subject: math
explanation: When we divide powers with the same base, nᵃ ÷ nᵇ = nᵃ⁻ᵇ. If a < b, the exponent becomes negative. A negative exponent means reciprocal: n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ (n ≠ 0). For example, 2⁻⁴ = 1/2⁴ = 1/16. Similarly, 1/10³ = 10⁻³. Negative exponents do not make the number negative — they move the value to the denominator. The laws of exponents continue to work for negative and zero exponents as long as the base is not zero.

brainstorming.question: What does 10⁻³ mean in words?
brainstorming.answer: One divided by 10 three times, or 1/1000 = 0.001.

brainstorming.question: Is (-2)⁻³ positive or negative?
brainstorming.answer: (-2)⁻³ = 1/(-2)³ = 1/(-8) = -1/8 — negative because the base is negative and the positive exponent 3 is odd.

brainstorming.question: Why must the base n not be zero in n⁻ᵃ?
brainstorming.answer: 0⁻ᵃ = 1/0ᵃ involves division by zero, which is undefined.

misconceptions.wrong: A negative exponent makes the answer negative
misconceptions.correct: n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ — the sign of the result depends on the base, not the negative sign in the exponent.
n⁻¹ = 1/n — it is the reciprocal, not subtraction.

misconceptions.wrong: You cannot multiply terms with negative exponents

realLifeConnections.title: Microscopic measurements
realLifeConnections.description: Thickness of paper ≈ 10⁻⁴ m — negative powers of 10 describe very small lengths.

realLifeConnections.title: Scientific prefixes
realLifeConnections.description: Milli (10⁻³) and micro (10⁻⁶) use negative exponents to express tiny quantities.

realLifeConnections.title: Half-life decay
realLifeConnections.description: Radioactive decay can be modelled with negative exponents showing shrinking amounts over time.

realLifeConnections.title: Reciprocals in recipes
realLifeConnections.description: If a recipe uses 2⁻¹ cup, that means 1/2 cup — negative exponents as fractions in daily life.

realLifeConnections.title: Computer memory fractions
realLifeConnections.description: A kilobyte is 2¹⁰ bytes; describing a fraction of a byte uses negative powers of 2.

activities.title: Reciprocal flip cards
activities.instructions: Write expressions like 3⁻² on one side and 1/9 on the other. Students match and explain why they are equal.

activities.title: Number line jump
activities.instructions: On a powers-of-10 line, start at 10³ and move left three steps to reach 10⁰, then two more to 10⁻². Record each value.

activities.title: Negative exponent simplify race
activities.instructions: Simplify 2⁻⁴ × 2⁷, 10⁻² × 10⁻⁵, and p³ × p⁻¹⁰. First correct team explains the product law used.

quiz.question: n⁻ᵃ = 1/nᵃ is valid when:
quiz.explanation: Division by zero is undefined, so n must not be 0.
